How the NIS survey design works

Source: vignettes/articles/nis-design.Rmd
nis-design.Rmd
library(easyNIS)
library(dplyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'dplyr'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter, lag
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, setequal, union
library(srvyr)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'srvyr'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     filter

nis <- nis_open(nis_example(years = 2019:2020)) |>
  nis_flag_dx(heart_failure = "I50")
#> duckdb keeps downloaded extensions and secrets in a temporary directory:
#> ℹ /tmp/RtmpS81fuG/duckdb
#> This is removed when the R session ends.
#> • Extensions are re-downloaded each session.
#> • Secrets are lost.
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = TRUE) (or create ~/.duckdb) to keep them (suitable for most users).
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to accept the temporary directory (and silence this message).
#> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives.
#> duckdb keeps downloaded extensions and secrets in a temporary directory:
#> ℹ /tmp/RtmpS81fuG/duckdb
#> This is removed when the R session ends.
#> • Extensions are re-downloaded each session.
#> • Secrets are lost.
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = TRUE) (or create ~/.duckdb) to keep them (suitable for most users).
#> ℹ Run duckdb(shared_home = FALSE) to accept the temporary directory (and silence this message).
#> ℹ See ?duckdb_storage for details and alternatives.
cohort <- nis_design(nis, cohort = heart_failure, keep = LOS)
#> Preparing the cohort survey design.

full <- nis |>
  select(nis_vars_design(), heart_failure, LOS) |>
  collect() |>
  mutate(psu = interaction(YEAR, HOSP_NIS),
         stratum = interaction(YEAR, NIS_STRATUM)) |>
  as_survey_design(ids = psu, strata = stratum, weights = DISCWT, nest = TRUE) |>
  filter(heart_failure)

summarise(cohort, total = survey_total(), mean_los = survey_mean(LOS))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   total total_se mean_los mean_los_se
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1  125.     17.3     5.66       0.229
summarise(full, total = survey_total(), mean_los = survey_mean(LOS))
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   total total_se mean_los mean_los_se
#>   <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1  125.     17.3     5.66       0.229

The example uses invented data. The two calculations give the same totals, means, and standard errors. The second fits the full sample in R so you can check the cohort calculation directly.

Hospitals in the variance calculation

Since 2012, the NIS has sampled discharges across hospitals in its sampling frame. For variance estimation, easyNIS uses the with-replacement ultimate-cluster approximation described in HCUP Methods Series 2015-09. HOSP_NIS identifies the hospital cluster, NIS_STRATUM identifies the stratum, and DISCWT weights discharges. The approximation uses variation among hospital contributions within a stratum. It uses no finite population correction. HCUP variance guidance

Why zero-contribution hospitals matter

For a domain total, a hospital with no cohort discharges contributes zero. Omitting it changes both the sample size for the stratum and the variation of hospital totals. Keeping one zero-domain placeholder per such hospital preserves those quantities.

The same argument applies to linearized scores for means, ratios, and supported survey-weighted regression models. Non-domain discharges have zero scores, so their individual records can be replaced by a zero contribution for the hospital. Under this design and the same singleton policy, the placeholder calculation is exact for these estimators. It preserves the full-sample domain calculation under the stated variance approximation.

Why identifiers include the year

A hospital or stratum number can recur across years. easyNIS identifies strata and clusters within each year so reuse of a number does not combine sampling units. Original discharge weights represent the pooled period. For average annual totals, check coverage before annualizing the weights.
